q: What is the default isolation level in Postgres, and can a dirty read happen?
options: READ COMMITTED, and a dirty read never happens in Postgres
SERIALIZABLE, and dirty reads happen sometimes
READ UNCOMMITTED, and dirty reads happen often
REPEATABLE READ, and dirty reads happen only on replicas
why: A dirty read means seeing someone's unfinished work. Postgres does not allow it at any level.

q: In READ COMMITTED, you run the same SELECT twice in one transaction and get different answers. What is this called?
options: A dirty read
A non-repeatable read
A deadlock
A write skew
why: READ COMMITTED takes a new picture for each statement. REPEATABLE READ takes one picture per transaction.

q: Two people each read balance 100, add 50 in code, and write back 150. What is lost?
options: Nothing, the balance is 200
The whole row is deleted
One of the two additions. This is a lost update
The transaction is aborted
why: Do the math in the UPDATE (`balance = balance + 50`) or take a lock.

q: Two transactions each check that at least 2 doctors are on call, and each takes a different doctor off call. Now nobody is on call. What is this, and what stops it?
options: A phantom read. READ COMMITTED stops it
A dirty read. Locks stop it
A deadlock. A shorter timeout stops it
Write skew. Only SERIALIZABLE stops it
why: Both transactions read the same rows and each write a different row. Both checks were right, and the rule broke.

q: A SERIALIZABLE transaction fails with error 40001. What should your code do?
options: Run the whole transaction again from BEGIN, and give up after a few tries
Ignore the error and continue
Retry only the last statement
Switch to READ UNCOMMITTED
why: A serialization error means: this one lost. You must retry.
